BLM’S REQUEST FOR REMAND DENIED
On October 20, 2005, counsel of record for the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), filed
BLM’s Request For Remand To Issue A New Proposed Decision (“Request”). In response
thereto, the undersigned conducted a telephone conference on October 21, 2005, in order to
discuss the legal and procedural implications of said request. In attendance at the conference, in
addition to the undersigned, were the following: Todd C. Tucci, Esq., on behalf of the
Appellants, and Kenneth M. Sebby, Esq., on behalf of BLM.
In its October 21st request, BLM seeks the following procedural remedy:
Under the circumstances, in order to avoid additional litigation, and to correct said
procedural deficiencies regarding the rangeland development projects, the BLM requests
an Order remanding the above-captioned consolidated matters to the Field Manager,
Owyhee Field Office, Bureau of Land Management, Idaho, for the purpose of issuing a
new proposed decision consistent with existing laws (including NEPA), regulations,
internal guidance and available data. The BLM further requests an Order that the
portions of the April 22, 2005 Final Decision which have not been stayed (Interim
Grazing System), remain in effect pending BLM’s issuance of a new proposed decision
herein. (footnote omitted; BLM’s Request, pp. 3-4).
Previously, on July 5, 2005, the undersigned had issued an Order, which consolidated the instant
dockets and which granted, in part, Appellants’ previously filed Petition for Stay. In that Order, I
stayed that portion of BLM’s April 22, 2005, Final Decision, which implicated certain,
enumerated range improvement projects. The legal basis for that partial stay was putative
noncompliance with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) in BLM’s underlying
Environmental Assessment (EA), as it related to the proposed range improvements. However,
because BLM’s Final Decision also served to reduce the number of active AUM’s, my July 5th
4

Order did not stay the interim grazing system portion of that decision.
In its October 21st filing, BLM requests that I now issue an Order which would accomplish the
following two objectives: (1) affirm, on the merits, the grazing system portion of the April 22,
2005, Final Decision, based upon the ground that said portion of BLM’s decision was not stayed
in my July 5th Order; and (2) remand to BLM for further decision making, in compliance with
NEPA, that portion of BLM’s Final Decision which implicated the referenced range
improvement projects.
The impediment to BLM’s requested procedural approach is that my July 5th Order was
interlocutory in procedural and jurisdictional scope. It did not constitute a final decision on the
merits, and it did not procedurally preclude the Appellants and the Intervenors from having a full
adjudicatory hearing on the record with respect to the interim grazing system, which was not
stayed. In this context, the Department’s stay regulations, issued under the auspices of the Taylor
Grazing Act, are modeled on the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP) pertaining to
injunctive relief, especially the requirement that a petitioner must demonstrate a likelihood of
success on the merits. Notwithstanding the regulatory requirement for demonstrating a
likelihood of success on the merits, neither a temporary restraining order (TRO) issued by a
jurisdictional Federal District Court, nor, by analogy, a stay issued by the Departmental Hearings
Division, constitutes a final decision on the merits. Rather, they are both interlocutory
determinations, which do not serve to preclude a trial/hearing on the merits. Stated somewhat
differently, even though the interim grazing system was not stayed under my July 5th Order, the
Appellants and Intervenors, as a matter of procedural due process, are still entitled to a full
hearing on the record, a full APA adjudication, with respect to the grazing system portion of
BLM’s Final Decision.
Consequently, BLM’s request for relief, as stated, cannot be granted, because it would deprive
the Appellants and Intervenors of the procedural right to adjudicate that portion of BLM’s Final
Decision which was not stayed, namely, the interim grazing system. For these stated
jurisdictional and procedural reasons, BLM’s Request For Remand To Issue A New Proposed
Decision, as stated, is hereby DENIED. The public hearing in this matter remains scheduled to
commence on December 12, 2005, in Caldwell, Idaho, as per the Owyhee Field Manager’s
notification letter dated October 14, 2005.
During our conference on October 21st, the parties and the undersigned also discussed other
procedural avenues that potentially could be pursued by the parties and the intervenors in order to
resolve this matter along the general lines requested by the government in its October 21st filing.
One such avenue would be a global settlement agreement, to include the Appellants, BLM and
the Intervenors, which would provide the procedural grounds for the issuance of a dismissal
without prejudice by the undersigned. Another, potential procedural avenue would be a Motion
To Vacate and Remand by BLM, which would require the concurrence of the Appellants and the
Intervenors. A third potential procedural avenue would be a Motion For Summary Decision,
although this approach would also require a stipulation of undisputed facts by the parties and the
5

intervenors. While none of the aforementioned procedures may bear ultimate fruit, BLM did
indicate in its October 21st filing that the Appellants and BLM, through counsel, have “...
initiated preliminary settlement discussions which have not yet extended to the intervenors.”
(BLM’s Request, p. 3). At the conclusion of our telephone conference both Mr. Tucci and Mr.
Sebby indicated that they would continue to pursue a settlement-related dialogue.
James H. Heffernan
Administrative Law Judge
